question: What makes a returning theme sound unresolved rather than reassuring?
intro: A funeral march in C minor repeatedly gives way to a long violin melody in a remote major key. Follow the difference between a return of the march and a real resolution: this movement ends before the symphony has answered its opening.

sections.label: Exposition · renewed conflict
sections.mNote: march rhythms interrupt the lyrical alternative

sections.label: Development · lyrical expansion
sections.mNote: lyrical material expanded through changing tonal regions

cues.title: A funeral before resurrection
cues.text: The symphony begins in C minor, with a movement marked “Allegro maestoso” and “with thoroughly serious and solemn expression”. The opening belongs to the orchestra alone; the voices wait until the fourth movement.
cues.evidence: Full score, movement I heading and movement sequence. The file begins with a low-level lead-in; this note does not time the first attack.

cues.title: The bass is the subject
cues.text: In the opening, cellos and double basses carry forceful melodic gestures beneath string tremolo. Follow their rises, falls and intervening rests: the lowest line is not merely supporting a tune somewhere above it.
cues.evidence: Full score, opening page. The report shows the first sustained rise from the lead-in at 0:15; this is an opening-passage description, not a bar alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A growing orchestral weight
cues.text: The opening gathers weight over several phrases. Listen for the short gestures joining into a larger span, rather than treating each accent as a new beginning.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from about −33 dB at 0:25 to −17 dB at 1:20–1:30. The measurement supports the broad growth, not an instrument count.

cues.title: A crest and withdrawal
cues.text: This first large surge is followed by a marked withdrawal. Keep the march rhythm in mind as the weight recedes: a quieter passage need not mean that the argument has ended.
cues.evidence: An early high window occurs at 2:05; level falls from −6.1 dB there to −22.3 dB at 2:20.

cues.title: An alternative to the march
cues.text: The lyrical subject draws a longer line above the bass. Mahler places its first statement in E major, far from the opening C minor; the contrast changes the harmonic setting as well as the manner of singing.
cues.evidence: Full score p. 8, rehearsal 3, gives the long violin line and E-major harmony. The quieter 2:20–3:00 stretch and novelty at 2:44 anchor the approximate region; the machine’s dominant-heavy key labels are not adopted.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The contrast does not settle
cues.text: The early lyrical alternative gives way to renewed movement and sharper contrasts. Listen for the difference between the connected violin phrase and the shorter figures that keep breaking the music into gestures.
cues.evidence: Full score, the material after rehearsal 3; analysis boundaries at 3:04 and 3:18 surround a rise and sharp fall. The section boundary is provisional.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Pressure held across phrases
cues.text: A broad, sustained stretch of stronger sound replaces the earlier retreat. Listen across its repeated accents for the larger phrase, and distinguish a continuing build from a succession of separate climaxes.
cues.evidence: The report stays around −8 to −10 dB from 4:00 to 4:30, before dropping towards −23 dB at 4:45.

cues.title: A movement from 1888
cues.text: Mahler completed the early form of this movement in 1888, years before the symphony was finished. The title Todtenfeier means a funeral ceremony; the final symphonic version includes revisions made in 1894.
cues.evidence: Mahler Foundation, composition and manuscript chronology: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-history/

cues.title: Small figures retain their force
cues.text: Through the quieter writing, keep track of the brief rhythmic cells inherited from the opening. A motive can preserve its identity when its volume, register and instrumental colour change.
cues.evidence: A general listening comparison grounded in the movement’s recurring march figures. The report places a quieter stretch at 4:40–5:55; no particular motive entrance is timed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Lyrical material opens out
cues.text: The central span expands the lyrical side of the movement rather than abandoning it. Its longer phrases pass through changing tonal surroundings, so recognition of the melody need not imply a return to its first key.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation describes the second subject launching a development in C major. The quiet point at 5:50, renewed rise after 6:00 and changes at 6:20 and 6:34 locate this broader span provisionally.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Continuity across a changed colour
cues.text: Listen through the change of colour for what remains connected: the direction of the melodic line, the length of its sustained notes and the bass beneath them. Harmonic movement can transform a phrase without replacing its contour.
cues.evidence: The strongest novelty peak is 6:34. The report confirms a substantial change near this note, but cannot identify the individual orchestral lines; those are listening targets, not detected events.

cues.title: A restrained middle crest
cues.text: The lyrical stretch rises modestly and then recedes again. Compare this smaller wave with the earlier massed surges: Mahler can give a phrase direction without bringing the whole orchestra to a climax.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises towards −19.4 dB at 7:20 and falls to about −30 dB at 7:45–7:50, substantially below the earlier 2:05 and 4:00–4:30 windows.

cues.title: The opera house in Hamburg
cues.text: From 1891 to 1897 Mahler conducted at Hamburg’s Stadttheater. The Second Symphony took shape alongside that operatic work, with much of the composing concentrated in the summer months rather than the theatre season.
cues.evidence: Mahler’s Hamburg appointment and summer work at Steinbach are documented in the composer biography: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Mahler#Stadttheater_Hamburg

cues.title: The texture gathers pressure
cues.text: The surrounding passage builds from its restrained level into a more forceful span. Follow how much time the rise occupies: the pressure accumulates over phrases rather than arriving with a single accent.
cues.evidence: Level rises from about −28 dB at 8:05 to −14 dB at 8:40 and approximately −10 dB by 9:10.

cues.title: A pulse inside the surge
cues.text: In the busier passage, listen for the underlying beat beneath the rapid surface figures. More attacks within a beat can increase agitation without making every phrase proportionately faster.
cues.evidence: The report registers increased attack activity around 9:15–9:20, alongside the 9:14 novelty peak. It does not establish a reliable performed tempo.

cues.title: Another sudden reduction
cues.text: After a strong crest, the music drops back into a much quieter space. Listen to what survives the reduction: the continuity of a bass or melodic fragment can carry the movement across a change in orchestral weight.
cues.evidence: Level falls from −7.3 dB at 9:50 to −24.7 dB at 10:15; a structural boundary is detected at 10:12. The surviving-line suggestion is not source separation.

cues.title: Recognising a transformed fragment
cues.text: Throughout the development, compare short phrases with the two opening characters: the interrupted march and the connected lyrical line. Mahler changes their surroundings before allowing either to sound like a settled return.
cues.evidence: A movement-wide comparison based on the score’s development of both subject groups; no unique thematic entry is assigned to 10:40.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A brief crest before retreat
cues.text: A brief renewal of force gives way to a much longer withdrawal. Follow the falling intensity without losing the phrase: the music is preparing another span, not closing the movement.
cues.evidence: Level rises near 11:25–11:30, then falls through 11:45 to around −40 dB at 11:55–12:05.

cues.title: Revision before the premiere
cues.text: Mahler completed a new autograph score of the first movement in April 1894. The whole symphony’s autograph was finished that December; its first complete performance followed in Berlin on 13 December 1895, conducted by the composer.
cues.evidence: Mahler Foundation’s history gives the 29 April and 18 December 1894 manuscript dates and the complete premiere: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-history/

cues.title: From quiet to renewed motion
cues.text: The central crisis begins far below the earlier crests. Listen for the long accumulation from this restrained passage: the distance to the next great surge matters as much as the surge itself.
cues.evidence: The report remains near −39 dB around 12:00, rises to −25 dB at 12:35–12:45 and continues upwards through 13:20.

cues.title: Chorale against the march
cues.text: The development sets hymn-like brass writing beside the march’s more fragmented motion. A chorale means several parts moving in measured harmony; compare that collective tread with the opening bass gestures.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation identifies a six-horn chorale related to the Dies irae within the second development: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-1-allegro-maestoso/ . The report rises from −20 dB at 13:00 to −10.7 at 13:20, locating this comparison within the central build without identifying a horn entrance.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The largest central plateau
cues.text: The long build reaches a sustained region of strong sound. Listen for changing phrase shapes within it: an extended climax can contain several arrivals without providing a final resolution.
cues.evidence: Four of the five highest listed windows lie between 14:00 and 15:05; the highest is 14:30. This compares relative level within this recording only.

cues.title: A crest is not a cadence
cues.text: Separate intensity from harmonic completion. Even at the strongest point, a phrase can still be directed towards another chord; listen for where the bass appears to settle, not simply where the sound becomes largest.
cues.evidence: A general harmonic listening question placed within the measured 14:00–15:15 high-level region; it does not identify a particular chord from audio.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The march returns after crisis
cues.text: The recapitulation brings back the opening’s forceful gestures after the long central struggle. Recognition does not remove their interruptions: the returning march still has to confront the lyrical alternative.
cues.evidence: The report drops sharply around 15:20–15:25, with novelty at 15:24, then resumes the opening’s characteristic pitch and level profile. Score form supports a provisional recapitulation region, not an exact first bar.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Remember the lowest voice
cues.text: Compare the returning march with the beginning by following the bass again. Its attacks and rests can reveal the return more clearly than the changing colours higher in the orchestra.
cues.evidence: The score restores the opening material in the recapitulation. The report rises from −19.9 dB at 15:40 to −11.3 at 16:15, anchoring this comparison within the renewed march build. The analysis does not isolate cellos or basses.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The return relinquishes weight
cues.text: The renewed march has its own crest and withdrawal. Listen across the reduction for the longer lyrical manner returning: the two subject types are still being set against one another.
cues.evidence: Level falls from −8.9 dB at 16:35 to about −21 dB at 16:45; the following sustained E-major region agrees with the score’s lyrical return. Individual notes are not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The remote key survives
cues.text: The lyrical subject returns in E major rather than being absorbed into C major. That unusual return preserves the distance between the movement’s two tonal worlds instead of reconciling them in the home key.
cues.evidence: The score’s recapitulated lyrical subject retains E major. The 17:06 boundary and sustained E-centred estimates through 18:15 corroborate the broad region, not an individual chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A premiere without the voices
cues.text: Berlin first heard the symphony’s opening three movements on 4 March 1895. The December premiere added “Urlicht” and the choral finale: the earlier audience heard the orchestral questions without the work’s vocal conclusion.
cues.evidence: Mahler Foundation, first partial and complete performances: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-history/

cues.title: The coda turns back
cues.text: The final span turns from the lyrical alternative towards the funeral movement’s closing business. Compare the opening’s broken gestures with the fragments that remain: the movement does not end with a broad major-key hymn.
cues.evidence: The cluster of changes at 18:22, 18:34 and 18:40 leads to a deep withdrawal near 18:50. The score returns to C-minor closing material; the coda boundary is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fragments over a persistent bass
cues.text: Through the coda, attend to the space between phrases. A sustained or repeated bass can hold a tonal centre while the upper parts become shorter, leaving rests to separate what previously formed a continuous argument.
cues.evidence: Score-informed listening to the coda’s fragmentation and C-centred bass. The report’s restrained 19:05–19:35 region sits around −25 to −22 dB before rising at 19:40, locating the comparison after the coda’s withdrawal. No isolated pedal onset is claimed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: One more substantial rise
cues.text: The coda gathers strength again before withdrawing. Do not mistake this late surge for the finale’s promised answer: the present movement is still completing its funeral march.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from around −25 dB at 19:15 to −8.8 dB at 20:20, then falls to −25.5 dB at 20:40.

cues.title: Five minutes in the score
cues.text: At the end of this movement Mahler writes that a pause of at least five minutes should follow. The instruction separates the funeral ceremony from the smaller dance movement; it is not a silence contained in this audio file.
cues.evidence: Full score p. 56: “Hier folgt eine Pause von mindestens 5 Minuten.” The analysed file lasts 22:10 and contains no five-minute closing pause.

cues.title: A close made from remnants
cues.text: In the closing passage, listen for how much of the opening’s weight can be suggested by a short figure. The final gestures need not reproduce the entire march to bring its C-minor world back into focus.
cues.evidence: Full score, final pages and descending close. The report holds approximately −20 to −24 dB through 21:05–21:35, with repeated C-centred pitch-class profiles, locating the restrained closing span. This compares the opening without assigning a bar to 21:20 or accepting the machine’s major/minor labels.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The sound gives way
cues.text: The final gestures subside into the hall’s remaining resonance. Keep the end of this movement distinct from the end of the symphony: the next movement replaces the march’s tread with a dance in three.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −18.5 dB at 21:50 to −36.9 at 22:00 and −58.7 at 22:05. Movement II’s triple metre comes from the score.

transitions.title: The march yields to a long line
transitions.how: The opening’s forceful C-minor motion relaxes into the E-major lyrical subject. Violins draw a connected phrase while the bass retains movement underneath; soft horn harmony and woodwind colour replace the weight of the preceding tutti. Mahler asks the tempo to yield, making the change one of phrasing as well as key. The march has been suspended, not resolved.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 8, rehearsal 3, Im Tempo nachgeben. Level falls after 2:10; the 2:20–3:00 region supports a broad lyrical contrast, with novelty at 2:44. The exact opening bar is not aligned.

transitions.title: Short gestures interrupt the lyric
transitions.how: The long violin phrase loses its separate space as shorter figures and heavier ensemble writing return. Brass and winds reinforce rhythmic cells against the strings rather than sustaining one uninterrupted melody. The E-major alternative does not supply the movement’s destination; the return to march-like gestures keeps the exposition unsettled.
transitions.evidence: The score’s post-lyrical writing restores short orchestral figures. The 3:04 and 3:18 novelty peaks bracket a crest and reduction; this boundary names the surrounding return of conflict, not a single cadence.

transitions.title: A retreat makes room for expansion
transitions.how: The forceful writing recedes before the lyrical subject is expanded in a different tonal setting. C major offers a temporary contrast with the opening C minor, but the phrase continues beyond it. Woodwind lines, quieter strings and harp colour spread the argument over longer spans: thematic recognition is preserved while the harmonic route changes.
transitions.evidence: The Foundation identifies C major at the opening of the first development; score pp. 14–17 shows the thinning and wind/harp textures. The report’s 5:50 low point, subsequent C-centred span and boundaries at 6:20/6:34 locate the transition approximately.

transitions.title: A quiet beginning accumulates force
transitions.how: A long withdrawal resets the scale before the second development gathers force. The march’s short gestures and the measured brass chorale offer different ways of moving through harmony: one interrupted, the other chordal. Their expansion produces the central crisis through accumulated orchestral weight, not through the arrival of an unrelated tune.
transitions.evidence: The Foundation describes two development spans and the six-horn chorale in the latter. Relative level reaches a deep trough at 11:50–12:10 before the sustained ascent to 14:30. No horn entrance is assigned to the boundary.

transitions.title: The crisis breaks back into the opening
transitions.how: The extended central crest collapses, and the opening’s bass-led gestures recover their structural role. The returning C-minor march is recognisable through rhythm and contour, but its rests prevent a continuous triumphal statement. Mahler restores the conflict that began the movement instead of treating the recapitulation as its solution.
transitions.evidence: The score restores first-subject material. A strong level reduction from 15:15 to 15:25 and novelty at 15:24 support the approximate return region; no bar-level timing is claimed.

transitions.title: The melody retains its distant key
transitions.how: The renewed march withdraws and the connected lyrical line returns. Its E major is the same remote tonal alternative heard earlier, not the C-major reconciliation a conventional recapitulation might suggest. Softer string and wind writing permits the melody to expand without making the movement’s home key secure.
transitions.evidence: The score retains E major for the returning lyrical subject. The drop after 16:35, boundary at 17:06 and extended E-centred passage through 18:15 support a passage-level placement.

transitions.title: The lyrical alternative gives way
transitions.how: The lyrical line thins and the funeral material again determines the ending. C minor reasserts itself through low-register motion, short recollections and renewed surges; the coda does not introduce a new closing theme. On the last page, descending orchestral figures lead to clipped final gestures and Mahler’s written instruction for a long pause.
transitions.evidence: Novelty peaks at 18:22, 18:34 and 18:40 accompany the withdrawal into the coda region. Score p. 56 supplies the descending final figures and pause instruction; those final bars are not placed at the join itself.

Representative quieter development texture: wind phrases and harp colour over sustained strings; passage position is approximate.
The recapitulation restores the bass-led opening gesture; this entry highlights its string core, not a complete instantaneous roster.
The returning lyrical passage restores connected violin writing and restrained wind and horn colour.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
